To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

bilateral electrolytic lesions in the central nucleus of amygdala of infant rat pups severely impaired the acquisition of olfactory heart rate (HR) conditioning but had no deleterius effect on the heart HR orienting response (OR) or on the heart HR unconditioned response (UCR).
damage to the CeA severely impairs olfactory heart rate CR acquisition in infant rats.
the central nucleus is a necessary component of the neural circuitry for olfactory heart rate classical conditioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role played by the central nucleus of amygdala in the olfactory heart rate (HR) conditioning in the infant rats.
the role of the central amygdaloid nucleus in olfactory heart-rate conditioning in infant rats.
the role of the central amygdaloid complex (AC) in the acquisition and retention of a conditioned cardiac response (CCR).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the central nucleus is necessary for heart rate conditioning, but it is not sufficient.
the central nucleus plays a critical role in the transduction and expression of a conditioned cardiac response.
the central nucleus is not necessary for the development of the orienting response but is necessary for the development and/or maintenance of the conditioned response to a conditioned stimulus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amygdala is necessary for olfactory conditioning, and that the central nucleus may play a critical role in this process.
the central nucleus is a necessary stage in transduction of a CS into a CR, but not in transduction of an unconditioned stimulus into a UCS.
the central nucleus may be a necessary stage in transduction of any conditioned stimulus into a CR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the central nucleus is a critical structure for the acquisition of cardiac CRs.
the amygdala is involved in processing the emotional aspects of a conditioned stimulus and not its physical aspects.
the central nucleus is involved in the processing of conditioned stimuli regardless of sensory modularity.
